A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same T-POP research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original personalization experiments across multiple LLMs and datasets, including reward scores, judged win rates, learning curves and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds feedback-noise tests, exploration comparisons, alternative-judge evaluations, complex-preference experiments and latency measurements.

M1.justification: v1 describes sequential reward-model updates and frozen deployment after T interactions. Section 3.2 of v2 adds asynchronous background updates while serving subsequent queries with the latest available model, plus freezing at any interaction. The core token-selection rules, reward-model architecture and loss remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The four original datasets remain, but v2 broadens evaluation to mixed-domain interactions, corrupted preference feedback and three combined preference targets: Academic & Accessible, Structured & Empathetic, and Creative & Concise. These introduce substantially different interaction conditions and preference requirements.

E2.justification: The main comparison suite remains Base, Pref, BS16, LA and AMULET. v2 adds targeted controls: random, entropy-based and Boltzmann exploration in Table 8, and an untrained reward-model comparator in Table 4.

E3.justification: Existing main settings are retained. New protocols include varied label-flip rates and injection windows, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-235B judges, 500 mixed-domain queries with 50 online iterations, exploration comparisons at 20 iterations, candidate-size sweeps and query/token latency measurements. These are additional evaluation designs, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C substantially extend the original learning-curve, reward-weight and model-size analyses. Additions test adaptation after 5/10 interactions, exploration mechanisms, feedback-noise intensity and timing, evaluator dependence, mixed domains, intertwined preferences, candidate size and computational overhead.

E5.justification: The existing plots and statistical reporting practices are unchanged. New tables report point estimates without introducing run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Expanded discussion of the algorithm's uncertainty bonus is not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–3 retain their results, but v2 adds substantial new outcomes. Examples include exploration scores of 0.64 for T-POP versus 0.57 for Boltzmann, scores of 0.656 under clean feedback versus 0.493 at 90% noise, and query latency of 23.26 seconds versus AMULET's 11.25 seconds. New mixed-domain results favor T-POP on Qwen and Mistral but AMULET on Llama.

T1.justification: v1 provides equations and an intuitive bandit justification. Section 3.3 of v2 adds explicit regret rates, approximately d_eff times square-root T and L times square-root T, under named RKHS and DDMC conditions, and asserts convergence for T-POP. These substantially strengthen the theoretical assertions, although no T-POP-specific proof establishes their applicability.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: resolving cold-start personalization through online pairwise feedback, combining test-time alignment with dueling bandits, avoiding backbone fine-tuning and achieving data-efficient personalization. Added supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations distinguishing epistemic from token-level uncertainty, explaining sensitivity to noise timing, and attributing complex-preference adaptation to existing embeddings. It newly acknowledges dependence on reliable feedback and increased inference latency. It also makes stronger claims about evaluator independence and domain robustness than the new comparisons establish.

D1.justification: v2 adds a public-code link, documents diagonal covariance approximation in Appendix B and describes background-thread updates. The approximation is newly disclosed; the PDFs do not establish an implementation switch. Existing architecture details, hyperparameter values, dataset sizes and judging prompts are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds connections to Tokenized Bandit theory, neural-bandit approximation references and gradient-based robustness work. It replaces the Li et al. AlpacaEval reference with Dubois et al.'s AlpacaFarm and removes the Huang and Lin reward-learning citations. Section 6's broader RLHF and personalization positioning remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Language revisions are concentrated in deployment, theoretical justification and the reward-weight discussion; most existing prose and the seven-section sequence remain. v2 also updates front matter, adds impact, acknowledgement and LLM-usage statements, and organizes experimental details and new analyses into Appendices B and C.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text and references from single-column to two-column presentation, relocating and resizing existing displays. It adds nine result tables, reformats percentage reporting in Table 2 and moves the original hyperparameter table to Table 6. Existing figures are retained rather than replaced with new scientific plots.

improvement.justification: New exploration controls, alternative judges, noise tests and latency measurements make the method's support and practical limits more assessable than in v1. The gain is tempered by unsupported transfer of cited convergence guarantees in Section 3.3 and overly broad interpretations of mixed results in Appendix C. The added evidence provides a limited net improvement despite these weaknesses.
